quiz.p: Which of these is a green for a compost pot?
quiz.why: A papaya peel is wet, fresh plant waste, so it is a green. Newspaper, a dry leaf and an egg tray are dry, so they are browns. Picking one of those usually means mixing up the two groups: greens are wet, browns are dry.

quiz.p: Why should leftover cooked rice stay out of a small compost pot at home?
opts: It smells strongly and brings rats and flies
quiz.why: Microbes can eat rice, but in a small home pot cooked food smells strongly and brings rats and flies. Big city plants and hot heaps can handle it.

quiz.p: Priya puts the same peels in two jars. She mixes torn paper into jar B only. After a week, jar A has liquid at the bottom and smells sour. What does this show?
opts: Paper keeps peels drier and lets air in
Paper makes peels rot faster than anything
quiz.why: The only difference was the paper. It soaked up the liquid and held the peels apart, so air could get in and microbes that use air could work. Jar A had plenty of microbes, but they were the kind that live without air.

quiz.p: In the paper jar test, why do both jars get exactly one cup of the same peels?
opts: So the only difference is the paper
Because one cup is the most a jar can hold
quiz.why: In a fair test only one thing changes. If jar A had more peels, we could not tell whether the smell came from the extra peels or from having no paper.

quiz.p: Who does most of the work of turning peels into compost?
quiz.why: Bacteria do most of the work. Worms help a lot, but a pot with no worms still makes compost. If you picked earthworms, remember that they are the decomposers we can see. Most of the work is done by the ones we cannot.

quiz.p: Microbes that live without air are called anaerobic. What do many of them make?
quiz.why: Many anaerobic microbes make sour acids and smelly gases. Some also make methane, which has no smell but burns easily.

quiz.p: Arjun's compost pot is dry and dusty, and nothing has changed for two weeks. What should he do?
opts: Sprinkle a little water and stir
quiz.why: Microbes need water to digest food. A dry pot is too dry for them to work. A little water, until it feels like a squeezed sponge, gets them going again.

quiz.p: Why does a compost pot need holes in its sides?
opts: To let air in for the microbes that use air
To let the compost fall out
quiz.why: Air holes let oxygen reach the waste. Then aerobic microbes do the work, and the pot smells of damp earth instead of turning sour.

quiz.p: Food and paper in a dump can last for many years. Why?
opts: The garbage is pressed tight with almost no air
There are no microbes in a city
quiz.why: Microbes are everywhere, also in dumps. But without air only the slow anaerobic microbes can work. William Rathje's team found newspapers they could still read decades after they were buried.

quiz.p: Dumps often catch fire. Which gas, made by microbes that live without air, helps the fires start?
quiz.why: Anaerobic microbes in the dump make methane, which burns easily. That is one reason fires like the one at Brahmapuram, near Kochi, in 2023 are so hard to put out.

quiz.p: How can you tell that compost in a pot is ready to use?
opts: It is dark and crumbly, smells like damp earth, and you cannot see the peels
quiz.why: Ready compost looks like dark soil and smells earthy. Slime and a sour smell mean it needs more browns and air, and more time.

quiz.p: What should go on top of each day's peels in a compost pot?
opts: About twice as much browns, such as torn paper or dry leaves
quiz.why: Browns soak up the wet, make air spaces and hide the peels from flies. Water would make the pot too wet, and plastic would keep air out.

items.p: Which of these can go in a small compost pot at home?
items.why: Onion skins are raw plant waste, so microbes turn them into compost. Plastic does not rot, cooked meat brings rats and smells, and a battery is hazardous waste.
items.art: Four things on a table: onion skins, a plastic spoon, a bowl of curry and a battery.

items.p: Sort these for a compost pot.
items.a: see items
items.why: Greens are wet plant waste. Browns are dry plant waste and paper. Plastic and glass do not rot, so they go in dry waste.

items.p: Bacteria do most of the work of turning peels into compost.
items.why: True. Bacteria are too small to see, but there are so many of them that they do most of the work. Fungi and worms help.

items.p: A compost pot works best with a tight lid and no holes.
items.why: False. Without air, microbes that live without air take over, and the pot turns sour and slimy. A compost pot needs air holes.

items.p: Microbes that use air to break down food are called ____ microbes.
items.why: Aerobic means using air. Aerobic microbes make compost that smells like damp earth.

items.p: Dry things for a compost pot, such as torn newspaper and dry leaves, are called ____.
items.why: Browns are dry. They soak up water and keep air spaces open.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: dark, crumbly soil made from rotted plants
to break down because living things feed on it
a living thing too small to see with your eyes alone
an animal with no legs who eats dead plants mixed with soil
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These four words come up all through the unit.

items.p: Put the steps for starting a compost pot in order.
items: A grown-up makes air holes in the bucket
Cover the peels with twice as much browns
Put browns and a little soil at the bottom
a: A grown-up makes air holes in the bucket
Put browns and a little soil at the bottom
Cover the peels with twice as much browns
items.why: First the holes, so air can get in. Then a dry bottom layer to soak up drips. Then peels, covered so flies can't reach them.

items.p: Remember the paper jar test. Jar A had peels alone, and jar B had peels with paper. Which jar usually collects brown liquid at the bottom?
items.why: Peels are mostly water. In jar A, the water drains to the bottom. In jar B, the paper soaks it up.

items.p: What does good compost smell like?
opts: Damp earth, like the first rain
items.why: Good compost is made by microbes that use air. Soil bacteria in it make the smell of damp earth. Sour or rotten smells mean there is too little air.

items.p: In the paper jar test, jar B smelled less than jar A. Explain why. Use the words 'paper' and 'air'.
items.a: The paper soaked up the water from the peels and held them apart. So air could get in. Microbes that use air did the work, and they do not make sour smells.
items.why: A full answer says what the paper did (soaked up water, kept spaces open) and why that matters (air for the microbes).

items.p: Draw a compost pot that will not smell. Show the air holes, the browns and the peels. Draw arrows to show where air gets in.
items.a: A pot with holes in the sides and lid, layers of peels covered with browns, and arrows going in through the holes.
items.why: The drawing shows the three things a pot needs: air, browns to soak up the wet, and peels covered so flies can't reach them.
items.art: An empty outline of a bucket with a lid.

items.p: Mrs Rao, who lives in the next flat, says a compost pot will make the whole balcony stink. What would you tell her, and what would you show her?
items.a: I would tell her that a pot only stinks when it has too little air or too much water. With holes, plenty of browns and stirring, it smells like damp soil. I would let her waft the smell of our pot or of jar B.
items.why: A strong answer explains the cause of the smell and offers evidence she can check herself.

items.p: Label the drawing of an earthworm: mouth, gizzard, skin, worm cast.
items.a: Mouth at the front end. Gizzard a little way behind the mouth, where food is ground with sand. Skin all over the body, which the worm breathes through. Worm cast coming out at the back end.
items.why: A worm has no teeth, so the gizzard grinds the food. The skin must stay damp for the worm to breathe.
items.art: An outline of an earthworm with four blank label lines.

items.p: Why does chopping peels into small pieces help them become compost faster?
opts: Small pieces have more surface for microbes to work on
items.why: Microbes work on the outside of each piece. Cutting a peel into many pieces gives them much more outside to work on.

items.p: Which gas with no smell do microbes make when they work without air?
items.why: Methane is made by anaerobic microbes. It has no smell, but it burns easily, and it traps the Sun's heat in the air.

items.p: Newspapers dug out of landfills could still be read decades after they were thrown away.
items.why: True. William Rathje's Garbage Project found readable newspapers in landfills. Pressed tight, with little air and water, they had barely rotted.

items.p: A peel left on a compost pot rots in weeks. The same peel in a dump can last for years. Explain why.
items.a: In a compost pot there is air, so aerobic microbes work fast. In a dump the garbage is pressed down with almost no air, so only slow anaerobic microbes can work.
items.why: A full answer names the difference (air) and what it does to the microbes.

items.p: A family in Mysuru is deciding what to do with their wet waste.

views.says: We should compost it ourselves on the balcony. No truck has to carry it, and our plants get the compost.
We both work long hours and the balcony is tiny. It is better to sort it well and let the city's compost plant do the work.

views.who: Selvi, who collects the building's waste
views.says: Either way is fine, as long as the wet waste is kept apart from the dry waste. Mixed waste makes my work dirty and slow.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then say one thing another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and backs it with a fact from the unit: home compost needs no truck and feeds plants, while a city plant can handle far more waste and make biogas. It then admits a fair point from another side, such as Selvi's point that sorting matters most for both.
items.why: This is a real trade-off. Home composting needs time and space. City plants need homes to sort their waste well.

items.p: Asha's compost pot is dry and dusty. Nothing has changed in two weeks. What is wrong?
opts: It is too dry for the microbes to work
items.why: Microbes need water to digest food. When a pot is dusty, they slow down almost to a stop. Sprinkling a little water and stirring gets them going again.

items.p: An earthworm breathes through their ____. That is why worms live in damp places.
items.why: A worm has no lungs. Air passes in through the damp skin. That is why worms live in damp places.

items.p: Match each compost problem to its fix.
pairs: Smells sour, with water at the bottom
Big pieces still there after weeks
chop the pieces smaller next time
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each problem has a cause. Too wet, peels showing, too dry, and pieces too big each have their own fix.

items.p: Put the journey of a banana peel in order.
items: A banana plant takes up the nutrients through their roots
Microbes and worms feed on the peel
The peel goes into the compost pot
The peel becomes dark, crumbly compost
a: The peel goes into the compost pot
Microbes and worms feed on the peel
The peel becomes dark, crumbly compost
A banana plant takes up the nutrients through their roots
items.why: The peel is broken down by decomposers into compost. Plants then take up its nutrients to grow.

items.p: You must have worms to make compost.
items.why: False. Bacteria and fungi do most of the work. A pot with no worms still makes compost. Worms make it faster.

items.p: Draw two zoomed-in pictures: the inside of jar A, with peels alone, and the inside of jar B, with peels and paper. Show where there is air and where there is water.
items.a: Jar A: peels squashed together, water filling the gaps, no air. Jar B: peels with strips of paper between them, small air spaces, the paper darker where it has soaked up water.
items.why: A model drawing shows what we cannot see: the air spaces that let aerobic microbes work.
items.art: Two empty circles labelled 'inside jar A' and 'inside jar B'.

items.p: The middle of a big compost heap on a farm can get hotter than a cup of tea. A small pot on a balcony hardly gets warm. Why?
items.a: Microbes give out heat as they work. In a big heap, the heat is trapped in the middle and builds up. A small pot loses its heat to the air quickly.
items.why: A full answer says where the heat comes from (the microbes' work) and why size matters (a small pot loses heat fast).

items.p: Which living things make the earthy smell of soil and good compost?
items.why: Streptomyces bacteria make geosmin, the substance that smells of damp earth. They grow where there is air and damp.

items.p: Sort these: do they happen when microbes have air, or when they have no air?
items.a: see items
items.why: With air, aerobic microbes make compost and earthy smells. Without air, anaerobic microbes make acids, smelly gases and methane.

items.p: India's waste rules ask every home to keep wet and dry waste in separate bins. Why?
opts: So wet waste can be composted, and dry waste can be sorted and recycled
So the garbage truck has less to carry
Because wet waste is dangerous to touch
items.why: Mixed waste is hard to compost and hard to recycle. Kept apart, wet waste can become compost or biogas, and clean dry waste can be sorted and sold for recycling.

items.p: Before 1861, most people thought every living thing needed air. Then Louis Pasteur found microbes that live without air. Where in the paper jar test did you see signs of these microbes?
items.a: At the bottom of jar A, where the peels were packed and wet. That is where there was least air, and it was slimy, grey and sour.
items.why: A strong answer connects Pasteur's discovery to evidence the child saw: the airless, sour bottom layer.

items.p: Meena did the paper jar test. Her jar B, with paper, smelled worse than jar A. Give two reasons that might explain this odd result.
items.a: Perhaps she poured water into jar B, so it was too wet. Perhaps she used shiny magazine paper, which does not soak up water. Perhaps cooked food got into jar B. Perhaps jar B was pressed down much harder.
items.why: A strong answer looks for a second thing that changed, because in a fair test only the paper should be different.

items.p: Plan a fair test to find out whether chopped peels become compost faster than whole peels. Say what you would keep the same and what you would change.
items.a: Two same jars, the same amount of the same kind of peel, the same soil, paper and place. Chop the peels in one jar into small pieces. Leave the other whole. Check every few days how much peel is left.
items.why: A fair test changes only one thing, here the size of the pieces, and keeps everything else the same.

items.p: In a Hyderabad housing society, people disagree about the fallen leaves in the compound.

views.says: I sweep the leaves into a heap and burn them every evening. It is quick, and the compound looks clean.
The smoke makes it hard for me to breathe. Please stop burning them.

views.who: Kavitha, who looks after the society's plants
views.says: The leaves are browns. Put them in sacks and use them for composting the wet waste from our kitchens.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Use what you learned in this unit. Then say what is fair about one of the other ideas.
items.a: A strong answer uses the unit's facts: dry leaves are browns that help compost stay airy and not smell, and burning makes smoke that harms lungs. It also gives a fair point to the watchman: his work is hard, and composting must not just add more work for him.
items.why: There is a real trade-off between quick cleaning, people's health, and the work composting takes.

items.p: 100 grams of peels and paper turn into much less than 100 grams of compost. Where did most of the rest go?
opts: Into the air, as water and carbon dioxide made by the microbes
It vanished, and nothing is left of it anywhere
items.why: Nothing just vanishes. As microbes feed, they breathe out carbon dioxide and let out water, which go into the air. Picking 'vanished' is a common idea, but the stuff of the peel is still in the world.

items.p: Every microbe that lives without air makes a rotten smell.
items.why: False. The bacteria that turn milk into curd can live without air, and curd smells pleasantly sour. Bokashi bins ferment food without air, and smell like pickle, not rot.

items.p: Most of the microbes in your gut live without air. What do many of them do for you?
opts: Help digest the fibre in your food
items.why: Many gut microbes break down fibre that your body cannot digest alone. So anaerobic microbes are not all bad. They help where there is no air.

items.p: Draw the journey of a mango skin through the world: from the kitchen, to the compost pot, to the air and the soil, and back into a new plant.
items.a: A loop: mango skin into the pot; microbes feeding; arrows to the air (carbon dioxide and water) and into compost; compost in a pot; a plant growing; carbon dioxide going into the plant's leaves.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that the stuff of the skin goes two ways, into the air and into the soil, and that a plant takes up both again.

items.p: Your friend says, 'This bag says biodegradable, so it will rot in the landfill in a few weeks.' Using what Rathje's team found, what would you tell your friend?
items.a: In a landfill, garbage is pressed down with almost no air. Even newspapers and food barely rotted there for decades. So a bag that might rot in a compost heap may last for years in a landfill.
items.why: A strong answer uses evidence (the landfill digs) and the reason (no air) to question the label.

items.p: The smell of damp earth comes from a substance called ____, made by soil bacteria.
items.why: Geosmin is made by Streptomyces bacteria. Our noses can smell a tiny trace of it.

items.p: In a compost pot, which would become compost first? Put them in order, fastest first.
items.why: Soft, wet, chopped peel is easiest for microbes to eat. Paper takes longer. A coconut shell is very hard and tough, and can take many months or years.

items.p: Many families in Bengaluru compost in terracotta pots. Why does a clay pot work well?
opts: Its walls let a little air and water through
Clay is the only thing microbes can live in
items.why: Unglazed clay has tiny holes. Air can pass in, and extra water can soak out and dry, so the compost does not get airless and soggy.

items.p: When a city composts its wet waste instead of dumping it, its dumps make less methane.
items.why: True. Methane comes from wet waste rotting without air in the dump. Composted with air, the same waste makes carbon dioxide and compost instead.

items.p: Match each finding to who found it.
pairs: some microbes live without any air
newspapers can still be read after decades in a landfill
follow the smell of geosmin to find bacteria to eat
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each finding showed something about how waste breaks down, and who is at work in it.

items.p: Label the drawing of a compost pot cut open: air holes, greens, browns, ready compost at the bottom, tray.
items.a: Air holes in the sides and lid. Greens (peels) in layers. Browns (paper and leaves) covering each layer. Dark ready compost at the very bottom, the oldest part. A tray under the pot to catch drips.
items.why: The oldest waste is at the bottom, so that is where compost is ready first.
items.art: An outline of a bucket cut open, with layers drawn and five blank label lines.

items.p: A farm has a big compost heap. Which of these would let the most air into the middle of it?
opts: A pipe full of holes pushed through the middle
A plastic sheet over the top
Pressing it down with a roller
items.why: A pipe with holes carries air into the middle, where it is hardest to reach. A plastic sheet and pressing both keep air out, and too much water fills the air spaces.

applications: Families in flats turn their peels into compost for potted plants on the balcony.
Farmers spread compost and rotted cow dung on fields to feed the soil.
Plant nurseries sell compost and vermicompost in bags for gardens and pots.
City compost plants turn tonnes of sorted wet waste into compost every day.
Biogas plants let anaerobic microbes break down wet waste and dung in closed tanks. They make methane on purpose and burn it for cooking or to run vehicles.
Indore turns sorted wet waste into gas that runs city buses.
Engineers pipe methane out of some landfills, so it can be burned safely instead of building up and catching fire.
Old dumps in Indian cities, such as Perungudi in Chennai, are being dug up and sorted, so the land can be used again. This is called biomining.
Temples and markets compost flowers and banana leaves instead of sending them to dumps.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of microbes live in one spoonful of compost?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can now read the genes of the microbes in a sample, and they keep finding kinds nobody has named. Most of them have never been grown in a lab, so nobody knows what most of them do.

open_questions.q: How do the microbes in a compost pot decide who does what, and when?
open_questions.why_open: Bacteria send chemical signals to each other, and different kinds take over as the pot changes. Scientists are only starting to understand how this teamwork is arranged.

open_questions.q: What is the best way for a big city like Chennai or Bengaluru to deal with all its wet waste?
open_questions.why_open: Home composting, neighbourhood composting, big plants and biogas all have strengths and problems. Cities are still trying them out and comparing results.

open_questions.q: How long will the oldest dumps keep making methane?
open_questions.why_open: It depends on what is buried, how wet it is and how it is packed. Scientists measure it, but every dump is different, and many are decades old.

maths.problem: Kavya weighed her family's peels on a kitchen scale for three days: 400 grams on Monday, 300 grams on Tuesday and 500 grams on Wednesday. How much was that altogether? Is it more or less than 1 kilogram?
maths.answer: 1,200 grams, which is 1 kilogram and 200 grams. That is more than 1 kilogram.
maths.explain: 400 + 300 = 700. 700 + 500 = 1,200 grams. 1,000 grams make 1 kilogram, so 1,200 grams is 1 kilogram and 200 grams.
maths.context: This is about weighing a family's kitchen peels, to see how much wet waste could go into a compost pot instead of a dump.
maths.why_maths: Weighing turns 'a lot of peels' into a number we can compare and add up over a week or a year.

maths.problem: Here are made-up smell scores from the paper jar test, from 0 (no smell) to 5 (very bad). Jar A: day 3 is 2, day 5 is 3, day 7 is 4. Jar B: day 3 is 1, day 5 is 1, day 7 is 1. Draw a bar chart for day 7. What pattern do you see across the days, and what do you predict for day 9?
maths.answer: On day 7, jar A's bar is 4 and jar B's is 1. Jar A's smell grows by 1 every two days, so it may be about 5 on day 9. Jar B stays at 1.
maths.explain: Jar A went 2, 3, 4: up by 1 each check. If that goes on, day 9 would be 5, the highest score. Jar B stayed the same, so we predict 1. A prediction is a careful guess from a pattern. It can be wrong, so we check it.
maths.context: This is about the paper jar test. Two jars hold the same peels, and jar B also has torn paper mixed in. Every few days you score how bad each smells.
maths.why_maths: A bar chart shows the difference between the jars at a glance, and a pattern across the days lets us predict what comes next.

maths.problem: For every cup of peels, you add 2 cups of browns. Today the family has 4 cups of peels. How many cups of browns do they need? If they only have 5 cups of browns, how many cups of peels can they cover?
maths.answer: 8 cups of browns. With only 5 cups of browns they can cover 2 cups of peels, with 1 cup of browns left over.
maths.explain: 1 cup of peels needs 2 cups of browns, so 4 cups need 4 groups of 2, which is 8. With 5 cups of browns: 2 cups of peels use 4 cups of browns, and 1 cup is left. That is not enough for a third cup of peels.
maths.context: This is about the compost pot rule: cover each cup of peels with 2 cups of browns, such as torn paper or dry leaves.
maths.why_maths: Equal groups help us mix the pot in the right amounts, so it does not turn sour.

maths.problem: Meenakshi's compost pot is ready 8 weeks after her last peels went in. She stopped adding peels on 1 March. About when will the compost be ready? How many days is 8 weeks?
maths.explain: 1 week is 7 days, so 8 weeks is 8 × 7 = 56 days. March has 31 days. From 1 March, 30 days takes us to 31 March. 26 more days takes us to 26 April. 30 + 26 = 56.
maths.context: This is about the balcony compost pot. Once you stop adding peels, the compost needs some weeks to finish.
maths.why_maths: Counting weeks and days on a calendar helps us plan when the compost will be ready to use.

roots.context: We have been learning how microbes and worms turn peels into compost, and why air matters. Now we ask what compost tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In your test, the peels pressed alone went slimy and smelled sour. The same peels mixed with dry paper smelled like damp soil. Paper let air in, and microbes that use air did the work. So the smell of rotting tells us which microbes are at work, and whether they have air.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'garbage stinks', as if the bad smell were packed inside the waste. But the same peels smelled sour in one jar and earthy in the other. The smell depends on who is feeding on the waste, and that depends on air.
deep_truth.evidence: In the paper jar test, jar A, with peels alone, collected liquid and smelled sour within a few days. Jar B, with the same peels and paper, stayed drier and smelled milder, like damp earth. Stirring a jar every day also made it smell less sour. In dumps, where garbage is pressed down with no air, food and paper last for decades.

three.who_am_i: Your gut is full of microbes that live without air. They help digest the fibre in your food.
three.what_is_life: Every peel you throw away is food for millions of microbes, fungi and worms. Their meal becomes soil for new plants.
three.what_is_this_world: The tiny particles in a peel are never lost. They go into the air and the soil, and plants build new leaves from them.

roots.thread: A peel was once part of a living mango tree or tomato plant. Microbes and worms feed on it, and break it into water, carbon dioxide and nutrients. A new plant takes these up and builds new leaves and fruit from them. Then someone eats the fruit, and the peel goes back to the microbes. The same tiny particles pass from plant to microbe to soil to plant again, through countless lives. Many different beings are made, in turn, of the same one store of stuff.

teachings.teaching: Bhrigu came to understand that food is Brahman, the whole. From food all beings are born. By food they live. Into food they return when they leave.
teachings.link: A peel was food for us. In the compost pot it becomes food for microbes and worms. Their compost becomes food for plants, and the plants become food for us again.

science.text: Decomposers return the carbon, nitrogen and other nutrients in dead things to the air and the soil, where plants use them again.
Some microbes need oxygen, some are harmed by it, and some can live either way. Louis Pasteur first described microbes living without air in 1861.

other_view.view: A smell is just particles of certain gases reaching the nose. Microbes making those gases are following their chemistry. Talking of food 'becoming' us, or of microbes being 'at work', is a way of speaking, and adds nothing to the science.

practice.title: Breathe with the soil
practice.say: Let's hold a handful of soil from a plant pot, or ready compost. Bring it close and breathe in slowly through your nose. That smell is made by bacteria, millions of them, living in your hand. Now breathe out slowly. Your breath carries carbon dioxide, just like the breath of the microbes in the compost. Let's breathe in and out three more times, and feel that we are breathing alongside them.
practice.kid: Hold some soil in your hand. Breathe in slowly. That smell comes from bacteria. Breathe out slowly. They breathe out too. Breathe three more times with them.

The main test uses two cut plastic bottles, peels from one day's cooking, newspaper and a spoon of potted-plant soil, all found in most homes. how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, most people thought a landfill worked like a giant compost heap. A landfill is a huge pit or pile where a city's garbage is dumped, pressed down and covered. People believed that food, paper and wood soon rotted away there. William Rathje, an archaeologist at the University of Arizona in the United States, decided to check. Archaeologists usually dig up old cities to learn how people lived. Rathje and his students dug into garbage instead. In 1973, in the city of Tucson, they began sorting and recording what families threw away. In 1987 they began drilling deep into landfills and pulling out what was buried there. They found newspapers that could still be read, decades after they were thrown away. The dates printed on them showed how long they had been buried. They found hot dogs and other food that could still be recognised. Packed tight, with almost no air and little water, the microbes that rot food and paper could hardly work. A landfill turned out to keep garbage for a very long time, not to compost it.
how_we_found_out.who: William Rathje and his students, the Garbage Project, University of Arizona
how_we_found_out.when: The Garbage Project began in 1973. The landfill digs began in 1987.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: A landfill rots food and paper away quickly, like a giant compost heap. Digging showed newspapers that could still be read and food that could still be recognised after decades.
